            Description            
            
        
        
        
            
            Hollow cast in two parts. 
The eyes are inlaid with "silver" and copper and the pupils are filled with a black lacquer-like substance. 
The jewelled ornaments are inset with a few pieces of turquoise. 
The garment is decorated with engraved ornaments. 
The bottom of the pedestal is sealed with a sheet of copper decorated with the visvavajra emblem. 
 
Padmasambhava (Tib. Padma 'byung gnas) is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyankasana) on a double lotus pedestal with beaded borders. He holds in the right hand lifted in the gesture argumentation (vitarka-mudra) a five-pronged diamond sceptre (vajra), and in the left hand resting in the lap, a skull-cup (kapala). Padmasambhava is clad with his typical triple garment and wears his distinctive lotus hat.
 
On the back of the pedestal is a dedicatory inscription in Tibetan dbu can  script:

[Ligne 1]
// dus gsum sang rgyas thams cad 'dus pa'i sku gsung thugs // rgyal sras pad ma 'byung gnas sku bzhengs pa yis
[Ligne 2]
mnyam med nam mkha' grags pa'i thugs dgongs rdzogs pa dang // ma gyur seṃs can thaṃs cad sang rgyas thob par shog // // 

"Through the making of this statue of Padmasambhava, son of the Victors and incarnation of the Body, Speech and Mind of all the buddhas, may the intention of the unequalled Nam mkha' grags pa be perfectly accomplished, and may all sentient beings, our past mothers, obtain buddhahood!" 
[French translation by Amy Heller: "Par la fabrication de cette image de Padmasambhava, fils victorieux incarnation des corps, paroles et esprits de tous les Buddhas du Passé, Présent et de l'Avenir, puisse l'intention de l'incomparable Nam-mkha' grags-pa s'accomplir parfaitement, et puissent tous les êtres sensibles, nos mères passées, obtenir l'état de Bouddha". (L'expression "intention parfaitement accompli" est spécifique à une consécration après la mort de quelqu'un, pour que toute mauvaise renaissance soit écartée).].
 
Padmasambhava was a famous Indian tantric adept who lived in the eight century and who, together with Santaraksita and Kamalasila, was instrumental in the propagation of Buddhism in Tibet. The rNying ma school or “ancient translation school” is based on the teachings of the Padmasambhava, who was later deified of whom they worship eight different manifestations.
 
According to the style this image dates likely from the 16th century. Nam mkha’ grags pa’, in whose commemoration this image was commissioned, therefore cannot be identical with the famous teacher of sNar thang who lived in the middle of the thirteen century (BA 536) or the other teacher who lived towards the end of the fourteenth century (BA 749).

            Bodhisattva Maitreya - the Future Buddha displaying the gesture of charity (varada-mudra)

Copper with remains of gilt; hollow cast in one part. 
The separately cast lotus pedestal is lost. 
The jewelled ornaments are inset with semi-precious stones, namely turquoise, coral, lapis lazuli and red granat. 
The bottom of the image is not sealed. 
 
The Bodhisattva (Tib. Byams pa), the Future Buddha is depicted as crowned and jewelled Bodhisattva in the sambhogakaya aspect. He is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyanka). He extends the right hand in the gesture of charity (varada-mudra) and displays with the uplifted left hand the gesture of argumentation (vitarka-mudra). As indicated by the projections at the upper arms, originally the two hands held each the stalk of a lotus flower (padma) or a nagakesara twig attached to the shoulders, one of them possibly decorated with a water-jar (kamandalu). Maitreya is extensively covered with inset ornaments, namely a five-pointed crown with the head of a hornedgaruda (Tib. Khyung) in the centre and the dharmacakra emblem above, a pair of elaborately worked earrings, two necklaces with attached pendants, ornaments at upper arms and bracelets, ornaments on the lower legs and anklets. This image is also identified as Bodhisattva Maitreya by the small stupa emblem attached to the top of the crown of matted hair (jatamukuta). The emblem on the forehead is possibly a ratnayupa. This symbol of keeping awake the memory of the Law (dharma) is described in the Bodhisattva-Avadanakalpalata and occurs on the forehead of other Maitreya images as well.
 
This image of Maitreya is the work of Newar craftsmen living mostly in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal and dates from the Early Malla Period (1200–1479) and dates approximately from around 1400 AD.

            Description            
            
        
        
        
            
            Gilt sheets of hammered copper; assembled from several parts and decorated with engraved ornaments. 
The crowns and the other jewelled ornaments are inset with turquoise, coral and glass underlaid with red foil. 

These images form a pair of male Bodhisattva deities composed of Vajrapani (Tib. Phyag na rdo rje) (left) and Manjusri (Tib. ’Jam dpal dbyangs) (right). The Bodhisattvas are standing in a slightly bent attitude (abhanga) on a single lotus pedestal. The right hand of Vajrapani is extended in the gesture of charity (varada-mudra) and the left hand lifted in the gesture of argumentation (vitarka-mudra). Manjusri has the right hand lifted in the gesture of argumentation (vitarka-mudra) and extends the left hand in the gesture of charity (varada-mudra). Both figures hold in the hands the stalk of a lotus flowering at shoulder levels and decorated with the appropriate attributes, namely the diamond sceptre (vajra) of Vajrapani, respectively the sword (khadga) of Manjusri. 
The Bodhisattvas are clad with a cloth tied around the waists with a belt. They wear princely ornaments, namely five-pointed crowns, a pairs of earrings, two necklaces, bracelets at upper arms and wrists, and pairs of anklets. The Bodhisattvas are set against a background composed of scrolling patterns and the heads against a nimbus decorated with rays. Three sides of the brackets are composed of rectangular shaped bars with scrolling pattern and the remaining side with a flaming border.
Manjusri and Vajrapani, together with Avalokitesvara Padmapani, are the most popular ones among the Bodhisattvas. 
This pair of embossed images originate from Southern Tibet and reflect a distinct Newar influence in the technique applied.

            Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara 

Hollow cast in one piece. 
The crown and the jewelled ornaments are worked without inset stones. 
The face has traces of painted cold gold and the hair traces of a blue pigment. 
The bottom of the pedestal is not sealed. 
 
The four-armed form of Avalokiteśvara (Tib. sPyan ras gzigs), known as Ṣaḍakṣarī (Tib. Yi ge drug ma) is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyaṅkāsana) on a double lotus pedestal. He displays with the main pair of hands the gesture of respectful salutation with the hands slightly hollowed (añjali-mudrā). Ṣaḍakṣarī holds in the upper right hand prayer beads (akṣamālā) and in the upper left a lotus flower (padma). He is clad with a cloth tied around the waist and secured with a belt. He wears princely ornaments of the saṃbhogakāya, namely a jewelled five-pointed crown, circular earrings, two necklaces, the upper one with an attached pendant, ornaments on both upper, bracelets on all four wrists and anklets. On the back is a mantra engraved in Tibetan dBu can script: //OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ//.

When the four-armed 
Avalokiteśvara (Tib. sPyan ras gzig) is associated with the ”great 
knowledge of the six syllables” (OṂ MAṆI PADME HŪṂ), he is called

In traditional Indian Sanskrit literature, this deity is variously named Lokesvara (SM 280; NSP 26), Lokesa (SM 83),  Avalokitesvara (NSP 2) or Lokanatha- standing (abhanga), in the diamond attitude (vajraparyanka), the noble attitude (sattvaparyanka) or the attitude of ease (lalitasana) (SM 8, 18, 19, 41).

The two necklace and the pair of bracelets are inlaid with "silver" and copper. 
The lips, the closed flower bud on the left shoulder and the lower border of the garment are inlaid with copper. 
The ornaments are additionally inset with turquoise, coral, crystal and other semi-precious stones. 
The garment and shoulder cloth are decorated with engraved ornaments. 
The face retains no traces of painted cold gold, but the hair has traces of a blue pigment. 
The bottom of the pedestal is sealed with a plate of brass decorated with engraved ornaments of the “Eight Auspicious Objects” (astamangala) (Tib.: bKra shis rtags brgyad): wheel (cakra), parasol (chattra), banner (dhvaja), water-pot (kalasa), pair of fish (matsyayugma), lotus flower (padma), conch (sankha), endless knot (srivatsa), and in the centre the visvavajra emblem.

She is seated in the attitude of ease (lalitasana) on a double lotus pedestal with beaded borders and rests the right foot on a lotus flower (padma).             Thang stong rgyal po ("tangtong gyalpo") (1361-1485) - famous builder of iron chain bridges

Hollow cast in one piece. 
The garment, hair and pedestal are decorated with engraved ornaments. 
The face has traces of painted cold gold and the hair has traces of a blue pigment. 
The bottom of the pedestal is sealed with a brass plate decorated with the visvavajra emblem. 
 
This image represents Thang stong rgyal po (1361-1485 or 1385-1464), a Tibetan genius of outstanding skills in many different fields, including architecture, sculpture, painting, medicine, etc. He is most famous for his construction of numerous iron bridges, of which several still exist.
 
He is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyanka) on a lotus pedestal. He is clad in a garment covering both shoulders and legs, exposing a naked chest. Holding in both hands a medicine pill, he displays with the right hand the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudra) and rests the left hand in the lap. gmu thog pa mon tan mgon po is represented as an old bearded man with features of a portrait like nature. 
 
Around the lower edge of the pedestal is the Buddhist creed in Sanskrit inscribed in Lan tsha script: // Ye dharma hetuprabhava hetum tesam tathagato hy avadat tesam ca yo nirodha evam vadi mahasramanah // The Lan tsha script is derived from the Devanagari and was mainly used by the Newar Buddhists.

        10.5 x 22 x 7.7

            Description            
            
        
        
        
            
            Hollow cast in one piece. 
The separately cast aureole (prabhamandala) is lost. 
The eyes and urna are inlaid with "silver". 
The lips, nipples, and borders of the lower garment (antaravasaka) are inlaid with copper. 
The cushion is inlaid with ‘silver’ and copper. The bottom of the pedestal is not sealed. 
 
The crowned Buddha is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyaṅkāsana) on a cushion placed upon a rectangular pedestal with beaded borders. The pedestal is supported by a yaksa flanked by a pair of lions (sinhasana). The pair of griffins originally occupying the corner positions are broken. The back of the rectangular pedestal is decorated with a pair of geese (hansa). He displays the “gesture of turning the Wheel of the Law” (dharmacakra-mudra), in the case of Shakyamuni referring to the First Sermon of the historical Buddha at Sarnath (Bihar, North-East India). Although images of Vairocana are sometimes also depicted with the dharmacakra-mudra, it is mostly the case with images cast after the 12th to 14th century or so. Earlier images of Vairocana in general displays the gesture of highest enlightenment (bodyangi-mudra). In this case therefore an identification as Shakyamuni is certainly justified. The meaning of crowned Buddha images in general is disputed. In the case of crowned images of Buddha Shakyamuni there might be a connection with the abhiseka ritual. 
 
At the two corners in front of the pedestal are small effigies of the donor couple in kneeling attitude, holding the hands in the gesture of respectful adoration (namaskara-mudra). There is a dedicatory dated inscription of two lines in Saradascript: / sam (5)4 deyadharmo yam/ sri-surabhiya/ tatha sardham/ sakabhiksu harisayasasya/.  “In the year 54. This is the pious gift of (the woman ?) Surabhi together with the Sakabhiksu harisayasasya”. [Translation O. von Hinüber]. 
 
The year is stated as 54 of the Laukika era which is equal to the year 78/9 of an unknown century; and which can only be asserted on stylistic grounds. Possible dates could thus be: 624/25 + 54 = 678/ 9,  724/25 + 54 = 778/9, 824/25 + 54 = 878/9, 924/25 + 54 = 978/9. The dates 678/9 and 978/9 can be ruled out. Of the two remaining possible dates the year 778/9 is the more likely one. This image is not from proper Kashmir but from the Gilgit / Hunza area.

            Yamāntaka or Vajrabhairava 
 
Brass with a darkened patina.
Hollow cast in two parts. 
The face is painted with cold gold and the hair with a red pigment. 
The bottom of the pedestal is sealed with wood. 
 
Vajrabhairava (Tib. rDo rje ’jigs byed) or Vajramahābhairava (Tib.: rDo rje ’jigs byed chen po) is a wrathful emanation of Mañjuśrī (Tib. ’Jam dpal dbyangs) whose head is placed at the top. He is shown with nine heads, the principal one being the head of a buffalo, thirty four arms and sixteen legs, stepping to the right with the right legs bent and the left ones straight (pratyālīḍhāsana), he is trampling on large number of various beings placed upon a circular double lotus pedestal. He holds in the principal right hand a ritual chopper (kartrīka) and with the principal left one a skull-cup (kapāla) and embraces his consort Varjavetālī (Tib.: rDo rje ro langs ma) who holds the same attributes as his principal ones. The other hands of Vajrabhairava hold a great variety of other attributes [Essen: II-316]. 

Sculptures and paintings were made according to explicit rules of iconography and iconometry or proportions. Of all types of sculpture, it is the casting of multi-armed tantric deities that is the most complex. Such was the case with the statues of Vajramahābhairava embracing his consort Varjavetālī.
 
The iconographic Sanskrit compendiums Sadhanamala (SM) and Nispannayogavali (NSP) contain no description of Vajramahābhairava or Vajrabhairava who are frequently represented in the Tibeto-Mongol pantheon (CBIT 15,  1416, 2264 [61]) and became the great protector deity of the dGe lugs pa tradition. This image corresponds with the description contained in the Śrīvajramahābhairavanama Tantra.

            (Tib. Sakya thub pa)  
 
Hollow cast in one piece. 
The separately cast pedestal is lost. 
The borders of the upper garment are decorated with engraved ornaments. 
The face has faint traces of painted cold gold and the hair remains of a blue pigment. 
The bottom of the image is sealed with a plain sheet of copper.

This crowned Buddha represents Shakyamuni. The crown emphasizes his aspect as “world sovereign” (cakravartin), the owner of the “seven jewels”: “wheel-treasure, elephant-treasure”, “horse-treasure”, “wish-granting jewel-trasure”, “wife-treasure”, “minister-treasure”, and “general-treasure”. Such images are often erroneously identified as Aksobhya – one of the five transcendental Buddhas – who also displays the bhumisparsa-mudra, but is usually not shown in monastic garments.

Hollow cast in one piece. 
The separately cast pedestal is lost. 
The crown and the jewelled ornaments are inset with turquoise, some of which are list. 
The face has traces of painted cold gold and the hair traces of a blue pigment. 
The bottom of the pedestal is not sealed. 
 
The four-armed form of Avalokiteśvara, known as Ṣaḍakṣarī (Tib. Yi ge drug ma) is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyaṅkāsana). He displays with the main pair of hands the gesture of respectful salutation with the hands slightly hollowed (añjali-mudrā). Ṣaḍakṣarī holds in the upper right hand a rosary (akṣasūtra) and the stalk of a broken flower, and in the upper left a lotus flower (padma). He is clad with a cloth tied around the waist and secured with a belt. Nor bu ’dzin pa) (right) and Ṣaḍakṣarī Mahāvidyā (Tib. Yi ge drug ma Rig pa chen mo) (left) (SM 6); accompanied by Ṣaḍakṣarī Mahāvidyā (SM 11).             Avalokitesvara Padmapani displaying with the right hand the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudra)

Hollow cast in one piece: figure closed, pedestal open worked. 
The eyes are inlaid with ‘silver’ and the nipples with copper. 
The garment is decorated with engraved ornaments. 
The bottom of the open worked pedestal is not sealed. 
 
The Bodhisattva, identified as Avalokitesvara Padmapani (Tib.: Phyag na padmo), is standing in a slightly bent attitude (abhanga) on a single lotus supported by a rectangular pedestal decorated with the figure of a dancing yaksaand a pair of lions (sinhasana). Padmapani displays with the right hands the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudra) and holds with the left hand the stalk of a lotus flower (padma) attached to the left shoulder. He is clad with a cloth tied around the waist and fastened by a beaded belt and carries the hide of an antelope (ajina) over the left shoulder. He wears ornaments include a three-pointed crown, earrings, a beaded necklace, a pair of bracelets and the “investiture with the sacred thread composed of jewelled beads” (ratnopavita). He carries a long  garland of flowers (puspamalaor vanamala) around the shoulders. A small effigy of Amitabha is attached to the crown. The distinct nimbus and aureole decorated with rays (prabhamandala) are characteristic for the late Kashmir style of the 11th century.
 
In correspondence with modern terminology, all male Bodhisattva images with a lotus emblem (padma) and the effigy of Amitabha in the crown or hair are identified in this publication as Avalokitesvara Padmapani (Tib. Phyag na padmo). In traditional Indian Sanskrit literature this deity is variously named Lokesvara (SM 280; NSP 26), Lokesa (SM 83), Avalokitesvara (NSP 2) or Lokanatha- standing (abhanga), in the diamond attitude (vajraparyanka), the noble attitude (sattvaparyanka) or the attitude of ease (lalitasana) (SM 8, 18, 19, 41).

            Description            
            
        
        
        
            
            Bronze alloys of different colours; hollow cast in one piece. 
The jewelled ornaments, eyes and urna are extensively inlaid with ‘silver’ and copper. 
 
The crowned Buddha is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyankasana) on a cushion placed upon a graded pedestal. He rests the left hand in the lap and extents the right hand in the gesture of touching the earth (bhumisparsa-mudra). The upper monastic garment (uttarasanga) is rendered foldless and covers the left shoulder only. He is bedecked with profoundly decorated jewelled ornaments.
 
This crowned Buddha represents the historical Shakyamuni and not one of the five Tathagatas. Crowned images of Buddha Shakyamuni are called  “headdress bearer” (mukutadharin). The crown emphasizes his aspect as “world sovereign” (cakravartin), the owner of the “seven jewels” (saptaratna), namely the “wheel-treasure” (cakraratna), the “elephant-treasure” (hastiratna), the “horse-treasure” (asvaratna), the “wish-granting jewel” (cintamani), the “wife-treasure” (striratna), the “house-lord”, i.e. “minister” (gehapati), and the “guide”, i.e. “general” (parinayaka). The panels of the crown are considered to symbolize the qualities of the five Tathagatas.
 
An identification as one of the five Tathagatas and in particular the crowned form of Aksobhya (Tib. Mi bskyod pa), who is traditionally depicted with the bhumisparsa mudra, can be ruled out because such images are only very rarely clad with monastic garments (tricivara). 
 
The art of Pagan in Upper Burma was very much influenced by the Eastern Indian art styles. In particular the Buddhist exponents of the Pala Schools were closely connected with the art of Pagan during the 11th and 12th century. Although numerous representations of crowned Buddhas are known in the art of Pagan, images inlaid to such an extent with silver and copper are extremely rare. The differences in style between North-Eastern India and Upper Burma are not striking but rather indicated by faint distinctions. Especially the treatment of the features and the upper torso are distinguishable characteristics.

            Cast in one piece, partly hollow.

The hollow cast upper torso of the goddess is sealed with a rectangular piece of gilt copper.

            Hollow cast in one piece. 
The eyes are inlaid with "silver" and the lips, finger-nails, as well as the borders of the monastic garment are inlaid with copper. 
The hair is painted with a black pigment. 
The separately cast pedestal is lost. 
The bottom of the image is not sealed. 
 
The Buddha is seated in the diamond attitude (vajraparyankasana). He rests the left hand in the lap and extents the right hand in the gesture of touching the earth (bhumisparsa-mudra). The upper monastic garment (uttarasanga) is rendered with a few folds and covers only the left shoulder. 
 
This image represents the historical Buddha Shakyamuni (Tib. Sakya thub pa) and commemorates the defeat of Mara (maravijaya) at Bodhgaya (District Gaya, Bihar, Northern India), which represents one of the “eight great places” (astamahasthana) of Buddhist pilgrimage. Uncrowned images of Buddha displaying the bhumisparsa mudra can only be identified as Aksobhya (Tib. Mi bskyod pa) if they are shown in the crown of emanations, form part of a group of the five Tathagatas, or are supported by a pair of elephants as vehicle (vahana) (Pl. 9306-29). If the Buddha is seated on a pedestal decorated with a vajra emblem he is identified as Buddha Vajrasana (Tib.: Thub pa rdo rje gdan).
 
Based on a metal analysis, this fine Buddha image has been attributed to 9th century Kashmir, while refuting at the same time such an origin on stylistic terms. Any comparison with Buddha images of secured Kashmiri origin rule out any possibility of such an provenance. The overall modelling and the facial expression would rather point to a Western Tibetan manufacture of the 11th or 12th century. The various Western Tibetan styles reflect beside local idioms influence of the Kashmiri schools and to a lesser extent also of the North-Eastern Indian Pala schools.

            Standing Vajrapani
Bodhisattva Vajrapani - with the “Diamond Sceptre in the Hand” 
 
Copper with remains of gilt; hollow cast in one piece. 
The garment is decorated with engraved patterns. 
The hair has remains of blue pigment, which is an indication that the image was earlier under worship in Tibet. 
The separately cast pedestal is lost. 

The fine modelled image od Vajrapani (Tib. Phyag na rdo rje) is standing in a gracefully balanced bent attitude (abhanga) on a circular stand with two tenons attached underneath. He dispalys with the right hand the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudra) and holds with the left hand a five-pronged diamond sceptre (vajra). The Bodhisattva is clad with an ornamental cloth tied around the waist with a belt and a sash about the tighs. He wears princely ornaments, namely a three fold jewelled crown, two earrings of different shape, a necklace with attached pendants, ornaments on upper arms, bracelets, and the "investiture with the sacred thread" (upavita).
 
In this study the following forms of Vajrapani are distinguished: 
*Bodhisattva Vajrapani (Tib. Phyag na rdo rje) in the bodhisattva attitude; 
*Candavajrapani (Tib. Phyag rdor gtum po), a wrathful form with vajra and tarjani mudra; 
*Nilambaradhara Vajrapani (Tib. Phyag rdor gos sngon can), a wrathful form with vajra and ghanta attributes; 
*Sri Ucarya Vajrapani (Tib. Phyag rdor u tsa rya), a wrathful form with vajraand ghanta attributes, and garuda (Tib. Khyung) emblems; 
*Mahacakra Vajrapani (Tib. ’Khor lo chen po), a six-armed and three-headed wrathful form with vajra and ghanta attributes, and naga emblems. This division does not take into account all the numerous Tibetan forms with other names.
